findings.title: Weak API Key Generation Using Hardcoded Secrets
findings.description: The MLX and llamacpp extensions generate API keys using hardcoded string constants ('JanMLX' and 'JustAskNow') as API secrets. These are not cryptographically secure and are reused across all instances. An attacker who discovers these constants can forge valid API keys for any model.

locations.snippet:
private apiSecret: string = 'JanMLX'
private async generateApiKey(modelId: string, port: string): Promise<string>

private apiSecret: string = 'JustAskNow'
private async generateApiKey(modelId: string, port: string): Promise<string>

findings.suggested_fix: Replace hardcoded API secrets with random values generated at application startup and stored securely. Use a cryptographic random number generator (e.g., `crypto.randomBytes()` in Node.js or Tauri's secure random). Store the generated secret in a secure location (e.g., system keychain or encrypted app state) rather than hardcoding it.

findings.title: Missing Authentication on MLX HTTP Server Chat Endpoint
findings.description: While the MLX server validates the Authorization header with `Bearer {apiKey}`, the validation only checks if apiKey is non-empty. An attacker can send any bearer token as long as it's not empty. Additionally, no rate limiting or session validation is performed.
findings.suggested_fix: Ensure strict equality comparison for the Authorization header. Consider implementing: (1) Rate limiting per client/endpoint, (2) Request signing with timestamps to prevent replay attacks, (3) Logging and alerting on failed auth attempts, (4) Timeout mechanisms for long-running requests.

findings.title: HuggingFace Token Stored in Application Memory Without Encryption
findings.description: The HuggingFace token in the download extension is retrieved via `getSetting()` and stored in plaintext in the `hfToken` property. If the application process is compromised or memory is dumped, the token is exposed.
findings.suggested_fix: Store sensitive tokens in system keychain/credential store rather than in memory. Only retrieve the token when needed for API calls and immediately discard it. Consider using a secrets management approach that keeps the token encrypted at rest and only decrypts during active API requests.

findings.title: No Authentication Required for Vector DB Operations
findings.description: The vector database extension provides no authentication mechanism. Any code that can call these functions (file ingestion, search, deletion) can access all vector collections and attachments without any authorization checks.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement access control checks for sensitive operations. Consider: (1) Thread-level isolation - ensure RAG operations are scoped to the correct thread/conversation, (2) File ownership validation - verify user/thread ownership before returning attachment data, (3) Operation auditing - log all vector DB modifications.

findings.title: No Authorization for Assistant and Thread Operations
findings.description: The conversational extension provides methods to create, modify, and delete threads/assistants/messages without any authorization context. There is no verification that the requesting user/entity should have access to a specific thread.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement ownership verification for all thread/message operations: (1) Check that the current user/session owns the thread before allowing access, (2) Verify message ownership before modification/deletion, (3) Scope list operations to return only threads owned by the current user, (4) Add audit logging for sensitive operations.

findings.title: Insufficient Input Validation on File Upload Paths
findings.description: The RAG extension accepts file paths for ingestion but performs minimal validation. An attacker could potentially use path traversal (e.g., '../../../etc/passwd') to access files outside the intended directory.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement strict path validation: (1) Use Path.resolve() and verify the resolved path is within an allowed directory, (2) Reject paths containing '..' or other suspicious patterns, (3) Use a whitelist of allowed directories, (4) Consider using file handles from the browser's File API rather than accepting arbitrary paths from the frontend.

findings.title: No Protection Against Concurrent Session Overload
findings.description: The extension managers allow multiple models to be loaded concurrently and only implement auto-unload of other models. Without proper session management, an attacker could potentially load many models simultaneously to cause resource exhaustion or DoS.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement session limits and request throttling: (1) Add a maximum number of concurrent load operations, (2) Implement rate limiting on load requests from the same user/context, (3) Add timeout enforcement for model loading, (4) Monitor and log resource usage (memory, CPU), (5) Reject load requests if system resources are critically low.

findings.title: Unvalidated Backend String Leading to Potential Deserialization Attack
findings.description: The `version_backend` setting accepts user input and uses it directly to parse backend configurations. Malicious input could cause incorrect backend selection or expose path traversal vulnerabilities.
findings.suggested_fix: Strictly validate the backend string against a whitelist: (1) Split on '/' and validate both parts separately, (2) Verify the version and backend type against known supported values, (3) Reject any backend string that doesn't match the expected format, (4) Consider using an enum for backend types instead of strings.

findings.title: Plaintext Storage of Session ID in Browser localStorage
findings.description: The llamacpp extension stores the backend type preference in localStorage without encryption. While not highly sensitive, localStorage is vulnerable to XSS attacks and can be accessed by any JavaScript in the same origin.
findings.suggested_fix: Consider alternatives to localStorage for storing preferences: (1) Use sessionStorage if the data is only needed during the current session, (2) Store sensitive settings in encrypted form using a client-side encryption library, (3) Prefer server-side storage of preferences when available, (4) Implement Content Security Policy (CSP) headers to mitigate XSS risks.

findings.title: Missing CSRF Protection for Chat Completion Requests
findings.description: The MLX server accepts POST requests to `/v1/chat/completions` without CSRF token validation. While Tauri desktop apps have some inherent protection, the lack of explicit CSRF handling is a security gap.
findings.suggested_fix: Add CSRF token validation for state-changing operations: (1) Implement a CSRF token mechanism (e.g., SameSite cookie attribute is already good practice), (2) Verify the Origin/Referer header matches expected values, (3) Use POST with CSRF tokens for sensitive operations, (4) Document CORS policy clearly.

findings.title: No Rate Limiting on Model Loading Endpoint
findings.description: The load endpoint can be called repeatedly without rate limiting, potentially allowing an attacker to exhaust system resources or trigger a denial of service by attempting to load multiple models in quick succession.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement rate limiting and resource controls: (1) Add a per-user or per-session rate limit on load requests, (2) Implement a queue for model loading with maximum concurrency limits, (3) Add exponential backoff for repeated failed load attempts, (4) Monitor and enforce memory/CPU thresholds before allowing new model loads.

findings.title: God module: web-app/src/containers/ChatInput.tsx exceeds 1800 LOC
findings.description: The ChatInput container component has grown to 1888 LOC, combining chat input handling, attachment processing, model selection, tool approval, and message submission. This violates single responsibility principle and makes testing/maintenance difficult.

locations.snippet: Large container component mixing multiple concerns: text input, file attachments, model selection, tool approval flow, and message submission

findings.suggested_fix: Split ChatInput into smaller, focused components: (1) ChatInputField - text input only, (2) AttachmentPanel - file handling, (3) ModelSelector - model selection, (4) ToolApprovalFlow - tool approval, (5) ChatInputContainer - orchestration

findings.title: God module: extensions/llamacpp-extension/src/index.ts exceeds 2200 LOC
findings.description: The llama.cpp extension's main file contains 2294 LOC with mixed responsibilities: model loading, backend management, inference execution, device handling, and settings management all in a single file.

locations.snippet: Monolithic extension file handling: backend initialization, model lifecycle, inference requests, device discovery, GPU detection, cache management, and parameter validation

findings.suggested_fix: Decompose into domain modules: (1) backend-manager.ts - backend lifecycle, (2) device-detector.ts - GPU/CPU detection, (3) model-loader.ts - model loading/validation, (4) inference-executor.ts - inference requests, (5) settings-handler.ts - configuration, (6) cache-manager.ts - KV cache management

findings.title: God module: extensions/mlx-extension/src/index.ts exceeds 1000 LOC
findings.description: MLX extension main file contains 1013 LOC covering model loading, inference, device detection, and Apple Silicon-specific optimizations without clear separation of concerns.

locations.snippet: Single file handles: Metal GPU initialization, model quantization, inference streaming, memory optimization, and device capability detection

findings.suggested_fix: Split into: (1) mlx-runtime.ts - Metal/GPU setup, (2) model-quantizer.ts - quantization logic, (3) inference-engine.ts - inference execution, (4) memory-optimizer.ts - memory management, (5) device-capability.ts - device detection

findings.title: God module: src-tauri/src/core/server/proxy.rs exceeds 2000 LOC
findings.description: The proxy module contains 2016 LOC implementing reverse proxy logic, request routing, response handling, streaming, and error handling all in one file. This is a critical bottleneck for maintainability.

locations.snippet: Monolithic proxy implementation: HTTP request transformation, streaming response handling, error translation, header manipulation, timeout management, and security checks

findings.suggested_fix: Decompose into: (1) request-transformer.ts - request building, (2) response-handler.ts - response processing, (3) streaming-manager.ts - stream handling, (4) error-translator.ts - error mapping, (5) security-filter.ts - validation/security, (6) proxy-core.ts - orchestration

findings.title: High coupling: web-app hooks depend on multiple service layers
findings.description: Web-app hooks (useThreads, useModelProvider, useHardware, etc.) directly depend on service implementations, creating tight coupling. Changes to service interfaces force hook updates across the application.

locations.snippet: Hook directly imports and uses: ThreadService, MessageService, AssistantService - tight service coupling
Hook depends on ModelService, ProviderService, UpdaterService - multiple service dependencies
Hook couples to HardwareService, LlamacppService - direct service dependency injection

findings.suggested_fix: Introduce abstraction layer: (1) Create service facades that aggregate multiple services, (2) Use dependency injection pattern in hooks, (3) Define clear service interfaces (contracts) separate from implementations, (4) Consider state management layer (Redux/Zustand) to decouple hooks from services

findings.title: Missing abstraction layer: Direct Tauri IPC calls scattered across web-app
findings.description: Web-app services directly invoke Tauri IPC commands throughout (tauri.invoke) without a consistent abstraction. This couples frontend to Tauri implementation details.

locations.snippet: Service implementations use raw tauri.invoke calls scattered across 332 LOC without unified IPC abstraction
ModelService contains 672 LOC with repeated tauri.invoke patterns - no DRY principle for IPC communication

findings.suggested_fix: Create IPC abstraction layer: (1) TauriClient or IPCBridge class that wraps all tauri.invoke calls, (2) Centralize command definitions and response mapping, (3) Implement retry/error handling at IPC level, (4) Allow for easy mock/testing by injecting IPC layer into services

findings.title: Inconsistent dependency injection patterns across extensions
findings.description: Extension modules use inconsistent patterns for dependency management. Some use direct imports, others use event listeners, creating unpredictable coupling patterns.

locations.snippet: RAG extension uses event-driven pattern with EventBus for dependencies
Llama.cpp extension uses direct service references and module-level state
MLX extension mixes direct imports with event listeners for state management

findings.suggested_fix: Standardize extension API: (1) Define ExtensionInterface with clear contract, (2) Use constructor-based dependency injection for all extensions, (3) Establish consistent event naming and payload schemas, (4) Document extension lifecycle hooks clearly

findings.title: Unclear responsibility boundaries: services vs containers in web-app
findings.description: The distinction between service responsibilities and container component responsibilities is blurred. Containers like MessageItem (442 LOC) and DropdownModelProvider (697 LOC) contain business logic that should be in services.

locations.snippet: Container handles message formatting, tool execution approval, reasoning display - concerns mixing presentation with business logic
Container implements model validation, provider configuration logic - business logic in presentation layer
Container orchestrates download lifecycle, progress tracking - should be service responsibility

findings.suggested_fix: Establish clear separation: (1) Move business logic from containers to services, (2) Containers should only handle presentation and events, (3) Create domain services: MessageProcessingService, ProviderValidationService, DownloadOrchestrationService, (4) Containers call services via hooks

findings.title: Missing configuration abstraction: hardcoded values and constants scattered
findings.description: Configuration values are spread across constants files and hardcoded in implementation files. Constants are defined separately (providers.ts, routes.ts, chat.ts) without a unified configuration system.

locations.snippet: Provider configurations mixed with UI constants - 354 LOC of hardcoded provider definitions
Chat-related constants scattered - no central config management
Extension settings defined in 390-line JSON - should support dynamic configuration loading

findings.suggested_fix: Create configuration system: (1) Config.ts with environment-based loading, (2) Separate concerns: API configs, UI constants, extension settings, (3) Support runtime config updates, (4) Centralize provider definitions in config, not hardcoded constants

findings.title: Circular dependency risk: providers and hooks interdependency
findings.description: Web-app providers (DataProvider, ExtensionProvider, etc.) and hooks share tight interdependencies. DataProvider manages global state while hooks read from it, but hooks also update state through services that feed back to DataProvider.

locations.snippet: DataProvider manages 258 LOC of state, consumed by hooks which call services that update DataProvider
Hook consumes DataProvider state and calls services that trigger DataProvider updates - potential circular dependency

findings.suggested_fix: Clarify data flow: (1) Establish unidirectional flow: UI → Hooks → Services → Backend/IPC → DataProvider updates, (2) Use Redux/Zustand to manage state flow clearly, (3) Document provider hierarchy and update paths, (4) Avoid hooks directly updating context they consume from

findings.title: Large hook files with multiple responsibilities
findings.description: Several hook files exceed 300+ LOC and combine multiple concerns. useLocalApiServer (352 LOC), useBackendUpdater (352 LOC), useTokensCount (270 LOC), and useModelProvider (509 LOC) should be split.

locations.snippet: Hook handles model provider management, configuration, updates - should split into smaller hooks
Hook manages local API server lifecycle, configuration, health checks - too many responsibilities
Hook orchestrates backend updates, downloads, version checks - should decompose

findings.suggested_fix: Split large hooks: (1) useModelProvider → useProviderConfig + useProviderModels + useProviderUpdates, (2) useLocalApiServer → useApiServerLifecycle + useApiServerConfig + useApiServerHealth, (3) useBackendUpdater → useVersionCheck + useDownloadManager + useUpdateOrchestration

findings.title: Missing adapter/bridge pattern between core and Tauri
findings.description: src-tauri acts as bridge between TypeScript core and native backend, but lacks clear adapter pattern. Commands are scattered across multiple files without unified request/response contracts.

locations.snippet: App commands mixed with app logic - no clear adapter separation
File system commands lack unified error handling and response contracts
Thread commands don't follow consistent command pattern

findings.suggested_fix: Establish command adapter pattern: (1) Create CommandHandler trait for all Tauri commands, (2) Unified response wrapper with consistent error handling, (3) Centralize request validation, (4) Document command contracts in schema file

findings.title: Cross-cutting concern: authentication/authorization scattered across codebase
findings.description: Tool approval, API key validation, and permission checks are implemented inconsistently across hooks, services, and containers without a unified security layer.

locations.snippet: Tool approval logic in hook - should be centralized
Model context approval scattered in separate hook
Tool approval UI mixed with approval logic

findings.suggested_fix: Create unified security layer: (1) ApprovalService for tool/context approvals, (2) PermissionGuard component wrapper, (3) Centralized authorization checks before sensitive operations, (4) Audit logging for all approvals

findings.title: Inconsistent error handling patterns across modules
findings.description: Error handling varies significantly: some modules use Result types, others use exceptions, some use error callbacks. No consistent error boundary or logging strategy.

locations.snippet: Rust error handling using custom error types - inconsistent with TypeScript patterns
UI error boundary component exists but error handling varies in services
Extension error handling not standardized with core error types

findings.suggested_fix: Establish error handling strategy: (1) Define ErrorResponse type across all layers, (2) Create ErrorBoundary for each layer (service, component, extension), (3) Implement centralized error logging/reporting, (4) Standardize error codes and messages

findings.title: Lack of clear testing layer boundaries
findings.description: Tests are co-located with source files but don't follow consistent mocking/stubbing patterns. Integration tests vs unit tests boundaries are unclear.

locations.snippet: Hook tests directly import services without clear mocking boundaries
Core tests mix unit and integration test patterns

findings.suggested_fix: Establish testing architecture: (1) Create test utilities and mocking factories, (2) Separate unit tests (isolated) from integration tests (with services), (3) Document mock strategy for each layer, (4) Create test fixtures for common test data

findings.title: Incoherent localization system: i18n scattered across layers
findings.description: i18n is implemented at multiple levels (web-app, docs) with different strategies. Translation keys and loading mechanisms are not unified across the platform.

locations.snippet: i18next configuration with dynamic namespace loading
Docs have separate i18n configuration not aligned with web-app

findings.suggested_fix: Unify i18n: (1) Share translation files between web-app and docs, (2) Centralize i18n configuration, (3) Create translation management CLI tool, (4) Document translation key naming conventions

items.title: Replace hardcoded API secrets with cryptographically secure random generation
acceptance_criteria: API secrets are generated using crypto.randomBytes() at startup
Secrets are stored in secure app state, not hardcoded
Each instance has unique secret, not reused across sessions
API key validation uses constant-time comparison
items.approach: Generate random 32-byte secret at extension initialization. Store in memory with secure lifecycle management. Update generateApiKey to use dynamic secret.

items.title: Implement strict authentication validation on MLX HTTP endpoints
acceptance_criteria: Authorization header validation uses constant-time comparison
Empty or malformed bearer tokens are rejected
Rate limiting implemented on chat endpoint (max 10 req/sec per connection)
Failed auth attempts logged with timestamp and source
items.approach: Use constant-time string comparison for bearer token. Implement simple in-memory rate limiter with sliding window. Add logging for auth failures.

items.title: Secure HuggingFace token storage using system keychain
acceptance_criteria: HF token retrieved from system keychain on demand, not stored in memory
Token only in memory during active API requests
Fallback to plaintext only if keychain unavailable (with warning)
Token cleared from memory immediately after request completion
items.approach: Integrate with Tauri's credential storage or system keychain. Retrieve token only when _getHeaders() is called. Use try-finally to ensure cleanup.

items.title: Add path traversal protection and input validation for file uploads
acceptance_criteria: File paths validated against whitelist of allowed directories
Path traversal attempts (.., ~, absolute paths) rejected
Symbolic links cannot escape sandbox
File existence and ownership verified before ingestion
items.approach: Use Path.resolve() and verify resolved path is within allowed directory. Reject paths containing '..' or starting with '/'. Add whitelist check.

items.title: Implement thread/message ownership verification in conversational extension
acceptance_criteria: All thread operations verify ownership before execution
Message list operations scoped to owned threads only
Delete/modify operations verify message author
Audit log created for sensitive operations
items.approach: Add ownership context parameter to all operations. Check thread/message ownership against current session. Implement audit logging.

items.title: Add access control checks to vector database operations
acceptance_criteria: All vector DB operations scoped to thread context
File attachment ownership verified before access
Collection access restricted to thread owner
Sensitive operations logged for audit trail
items.approach: Wrap vector DB operations with thread context validation. Verify file ownership. Implement audit logging.

items.title: Validate backend string format against whitelist
acceptance_criteria: Backend string format strictly validated (version/backend pattern)
Both parts checked against known supported values
Invalid formats rejected with clear error message
No path traversal possible via backend string
items.approach: Extract version and backend parts, validate each against whitelist. Use enum for backend types instead of strings where possible.

items.title: Implement session limits and load request throttling
acceptance_criteria: Maximum 3 concurrent model loads enforced
Load requests rate limited to 1 per 2 seconds
System resource checks before allowing new model load
Memory usage must be <80% of available before load
items.approach: Add load queue with concurrency limit. Implement rate limiter with token bucket. Check available memory before load.

items.title: Add rate limiting to model loading endpoints
acceptance_criteria: Per-endpoint rate limit: max 5 load requests per minute
Exponential backoff on repeated failures (2s, 4s, 8s)
Rate limit headers included in responses
Rejection with 429 Too Many Requests when limit exceeded
items.approach: Add RateLimiter middleware. Implement exponential backoff for failures. Return 429 with Retry-After header.

items.title: Refactor ChatInput container into smaller focused components
acceptance_criteria: ChatInput split into 5 focused components, each <400 LOC
Single responsibility for each component
Props clearly defined and documented
Container orchestrates but doesn't implement logic
items.approach: Extract ChatInputField (text input), AttachmentPanel (file handling), ChatInputToolbar (model/tool UI), keep ChatInputContainer for orchestration.

items.title: Decompose llamacpp extension into domain modules
acceptance_criteria: index.ts reduced to <500 LOC orchestration only
Each module has single clear responsibility
No circular dependencies between modules
Clear interfaces for module interaction
All tests pass and coverage maintained

acceptance_criteria: TauriClient/IPCBridge wraps all tauri.invoke calls

Clear, documented lifecycle hooks

acceptance_criteria: MessageItem reduced to <150 LOC presentation only

Consolidated F-8dff9e10, F-1f74fe1f, F-b88b5afc, F-72895412 as parallel refactoring tasks (god module decomposition). Level 2 (11 items): Authentication enforcement, token management, architecture abstraction. Level 3 (7 items): Authorization checks, hook/container refactoring, service decomposition. Level 4 (3 items): Large module decomposition (god module fixes). Critical path: API secret generation (F-7d74336a) → auth validation (F-de3ebc7f) → token security (F-1f437170). Architecture improvements can proceed in parallel. No findings deferred; all are actionable within development capacity.

codebase_map.architecture_summary: Jan is a local AI inference platform built as a Tauri desktop application with a React frontend. The architecture consists of: (1) Web UI layer using React 18 with i18n support, (2) Tauri native bridge providing IPC between frontend and backend, (3) Core TypeScript engine handling events, extensions, and model management, (4) Pluggable inference extensions supporting llama.cpp for general CPUs, MLX for Apple Silicon, RAG for document retrieval, and vector DB for embeddings, (5) Optional external API integration for cloud models (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.). The app runs entirely locally with no mandatory cloud dependencies.
key_patterns: Tauri IPC pattern - frontend communicates with core via Tauri commands/events
Extension plugin pattern - inference backends loaded as plugins
Event-driven architecture - Core uses typed events for all state changes
Model Manager pattern - centralized model download, loading, and lifecycle
Tool Approval pattern - MCP tools require user consent before execution
